headline: The Nursing & Patient Care Foundation
threshold: By Lesson 10, you can greet patients, say vital sign numbers, describe how a patient is, ask simple assessment questions, make polite requests and get help in Spanish, and start Nursing & Patient Care Lesson 1.

lessons.title: Sounds and Greetings
lessons.objective: Say Spanish vowels and key sounds clearly and greet patients formally at the bedside.
lessons.focus: The five vowels, ch, j, ll, rr, the written accent, and formal greetings

words.note: A man who is a nurse is el enfermero.
Use la paciente for a woman.
Vowels are short and pure: CA-ma, never 'cay-muh'.
The o is short and clean, never 'oh-oo'.
j sounds like a strong English h: he-RIN-ga.
The h is silent: al-mo-A-da.
ll sounds like y (SI-ya); r at the start of a word is rolled.
ch sounds like English ch in 'church'.
The written accent marks the stress: ha-bi-ta-CIÓN.
Stress the accented syllable: MÉ-di-co.
rr is a strong rolled r: dia-RRE-a.
su = your (formal). A man says soy su enfermero.
ll sounds like y: me YA-mo.
Formal: use usted with patients.

lessons.speaking: Greet a patient at the bedside, say your name and that you are their nurse, and ask how they are using usted.

lessons.title: Numbers, Time and Measurements
lessons.objective: Say numbers, clock times and vital sign readings in degrees, pounds, mg and mL.
lessons.focus: Numbers 0 to 1,000, clock time, and vital signs in degrees, pounds, mg and mL

words.note: Short for la presión arterial.
Same form for singular and plural: las dosis.
Use es la 1 for one o'clock, son las for other hours.

words.en: Per the doctor's order, you're due for 1 pill at 9.
words.es: Según la orden del médico, le toca 1 pastilla a las 9.
words.note: Le toca = you're due / it's your turn.
Always read the amount back from the label or order.

lessons.speaking: Tell a patient the time and read their temperature, pulse and blood pressure numbers out loud in Spanish.

lessons.title: Ser and Estar
lessons.objective: Use ser and estar to say who you are and describe a patient's condition and location.
lessons.focus: ser for who or what someone is, estar for a patient's condition or location

words.note: mareada for a woman.
cansada for a woman.
despierta for a woman.
dormida for a woman.
tranquila for a woman.
nerviosa for a woman.
Use with ser: es alérgico. alérgica for a woman.
ser for a profession, no 'una'. A man says soy enfermero registrado.
estar: a condition that can change. Ask a woman: ¿Está mareada?

words.en: Are you allergic to any medication?
words.note: ser: a lasting trait. Ask a woman: ¿Es alérgica…?

words.en: Your family is in the waiting room.
words.es: Su familia está en la sala de espera.
words.note: estar for location.

lessons.speaking: Ask a patient if they are dizzy or tired, ask if they are allergic to any medication, and tell them where their family is.

lessons.title: Have, There Is, Need and Want
lessons.objective: Ask patients what they have, need or want, and say what has to be done.
lessons.focus: tener, hay, necesitar, querer and hay que + infinitive for patient needs

words.note: Usually plural in Spanish: tengo náuseas.
tener sed = to be thirsty.
A feminine noun that takes el; tener hambre = to be hungry.
A feminine noun that takes el in the singular, so adjectives use the feminine form.
Common in Mexican Spanish; also la manta.

words.en: I need to wash my hands.
Per the order, we have to take your blood pressure every 4 hours.
words.es: Según la orden, hay que tomarle la presión cada 4 horas.
words.note: hay que + infinitive = it's necessary to.

lessons.speaking: Ask a patient if they have pain, nausea or thirst, and offer them water or a blanket.

lessons.title: Go, Do and Can
lessons.objective: Tell patients what you are going to do, what you do, and what they can do.
lessons.focus: ir, ir a + infinitive for care plans, hacer, and poder for what a patient can do

words.note: Many people also say los rayos X.
Also means the floor you walk on.

words.en: I'm going to draw blood from your arm.
words.es: Voy a sacarle sangre del brazo.

words.en: I'm going to ask you some questions.
words.note: Spanish uses hacer preguntas, not preguntar preguntas.

words.en: We're going to walk in the hallway.
words.es: Vamos a caminar por el pasillo.

words.en: At 10 they're going to do an X-ray on you.
words.es: A las 10 le van a hacer una radiografía.

words.note: Ask a woman: ¿Puede caminar sola?

lessons.speaking: Tell a patient what you are going to do next: ask some questions, draw blood from the arm, and walk together in the hallway.

lessons.title: Present Tense
lessons.objective: Describe daily shift routines in the present tense with patients and coworkers.
lessons.focus: Present-tense -ar, -er, -ir endings for yo, tú, usted, nosotros and ellos

words.note: la compañera for a woman.

words.es: Trabajo en el turno de día.

words.en: Do you cover my patients at lunchtime?
words.es: ¿Tú cubres a mis pacientes a la hora del almuerzo?
words.note: tú is informal, between coworkers. Note the personal a.

words.en: Do you eat well at home?

words.note: Ask a woman: ¿Usted vive sola?

lessons.speaking: Talk with a coworker about your shift: when you work, who covers your patients at lunch, and when the doctors come by.

lessons.title: Questions
lessons.objective: Ask patients simple questions to verify identity and assess pain.
lessons.focus: Question words qué, quién, dónde, cuándo, cuánto, cómo, por qué, cuál

words.note: cuántas before a feminine noun: ¿cuántas pastillas?
The answer word porque (because) is one word.
Use cuál with es for names, dates and numbers.
Formal, for patients.

words.en: What is your date of birth?
From 0 to 10, how much pain do you have?
When was your last bowel movement?
words.note: Many patients say hacer del baño for using the bathroom.

lessons.speaking: Verify a patient's name and date of birth, then ask where it hurts and how much pain they have from 0 to 10.

lessons.title: No, Never and How Much
lessons.objective: Answer with no, never, nothing and not yet, and compare more or less pain.
lessons.focus: no, nunca, nadie, nada, todavía no, más, menos and otro in patient talk

words.note: otra before a feminine noun. Never say 'un otro'.

words.en: I don't have the results yet.
Do you have more or less pain than yesterday?
words.es: ¿Tiene más o menos dolor que ayer?

words.en: Nobody explained the medication to you?
Do you want another glass of water?
You don't feel anything in your feet?
words.note: Spanish uses a double negative: no… nada.

lessons.speaking: Ask a patient if the pain is more or less than yesterday, offer another glass of water, and say you don't have the results yet.

lessons.title: Polite Requests and Commands
lessons.objective: Make polite requests and give simple usted commands to patients at the bedside.
lessons.focus: ¿Puede…? requests and usted commands like abra, respire, voltéese

words.note: Also la pulsera de identificación.

words.en: Can you open your mouth, please?

words.note: usted command; por favor keeps it polite.

words.en: Can you show me your wristband?
Press the call bell if you need anything.
words.es: Toque el timbre si necesita algo.

lessons.speaking: Ask a patient politely to open their mouth, take a deep breath, turn onto their side, and show you their wristband.

lessons.title: Words You Already Know and Getting Help
lessons.objective: Recognize medical cognates and use survival phrases to get help or an interpreter.
lessons.focus: Cognates ending in -ción, -dad, -ente and survival phrases for getting help

words.note: -ción words are feminine and match English -tion.
-dad words are feminine and match English -ty.
la intérprete for a woman.

words.en: Can you repeat it more slowly, please?
I'm going to call an interpreter.
words.es: Voy a llamar a un intérprete.
words.note: Use a medical interpreter for consent and teaching.

words.en: How do you say "pain" in Spanish?
I need help, it's an emergency!
I'm going to let the doctor know.

lessons.speaking: Tell a patient you don't speak much Spanish, ask them to repeat more slowly, and say you will call an interpreter.
